text: Root, children, leaves, depth; array storage and child arrays.
node i: children 2i and 2i + 1, parent i / 2

A binary tree starts at one root; every node has at most two children, a left and a right. Nodes without children are leaves (green). The depth of a node counts the levels from the root; the tree's depth is the deepest level.
A complete binary tree fills every level from left to right, so it fits in an array with no pointers: root at 1, children of i at 2i and 2i + 1, parent at i / 2.

title: A tree stored in an array: knockout tournament

text: A knockout bracket is a complete binary tree: countries are leaves, every match is an internal node holding its winner. Fill the nodes from the bottom up; the runner-up is the loser of the final, the weaker of nodes 2 and 3 (P4715).
abc bdi cj*
abdicj

For a general tree, store each node's children in two arrays lc[u] and rc[u] , with 0 (or a symbol such as '*' ) for "none". Depth is recursive: an empty tree has depth 0, otherwise 1 + the deeper subtree (P4913).
Letters can index arrays directly, since a char is a number (P1305).
Pre-, in-, post- and level order; rebuilding a tree from two orders.
A

lines: pre-order (先序) root, left, right A B D E C F
in-order (中序) left, root, right D B E A C F
post-order (后序) left, right, root D E B F C A
level order (层序) level by level (BFS) A B C D E F

text: The three depth-first orders differ only in when the root is printed: before, between or after its two subtrees. Each is a three-line recursive function.

title: Rebuilding a tree from two orders

text: BADC BDCA
ABCD
ABEDFCHG CBADEFGH
AEFDBHGC

Pre-order gives the root first, post-order gives it last; the root's position in the in-order splits the remaining letters into the left and right subtrees, and their sizes split the other order the same way.
Recurse on both halves (P1030, P1827).
abc cba

Pre-order and post-order without in-order do not fix the tree: a node with only one child could have it on the left or the right. Such a node shows up as a pair "x y" in pre-order that appears as "y x" in post-order; each one doubles the count (P1229).
Binary search trees, and trees treated as graphs.
left subtree < node < right subtree

In a binary search tree (BST) every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger. Searching or inserting walks one path from the root: left if smaller, right if larger.
An in-order walk lists the values sorted.
Inserting already sorted values makes the tree a long chain, and every operation becomes O(n). The library set keeps itself balanced (第17章); write your own BST to learn the idea.
Rank, k-th smallest, predecessor and successor are all one walk down the tree once each node also stores its subtree size (P5076).

Walking from a child back to its parent is allowed here, so treat the tree as an undirected graph: store every edge in both directions with vector<int> adj[N] . With n ≤ 100, run a BFS from every node and keep the cheapest total (P1364).

Depth, width (the most nodes on one level) and the distance between two nodes (up to their lowest common ancestor and down again) come from one BFS that records depth and parent (P3884). Drawing a tree in text (P1185) places each node by its depth and in-order position.
